b: Builds each picture like a film shoot — script, costume, props, lighting all decided before the first brushstroke — then paints a single woman in a period dress or a beret, half-lit, looking away, in oil so smooth the fabric reads as touchable. Hakujitsu-kai member; solo museum show at the Chiba Prefectural Museum of Art in 2022.
why: The most direct heir to Morimoto Sosuke's sealed quiet, except Yamamoto stages it: the light is cinematic and the mood is directed, which is exactly the 三重野慶/Casey Baugh side of the hush cluster.

works.t: ノエマの森にて (In the Forest of Noema)
宵の物語 II (Evening Tale II)

b: Oil-and-tempera paintings of young women placed in shallow river water, on wet stones, under forest canopy — a girl lying full-length in a stream with the current running over her dress, two women sitting apart on boulders in green shade. Tokyo Geidai graduate, Hakujitsu-kai member, Prime Minister's Prize 2014.
why: He is the Japanese painter who owns the figure-seen-through-water idea the collection already keeps in 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks, but with Morimoto's cool tempera surface instead of loose paint.

b: Close-cropped heads of young women in which the face is half-buried — under torn paper, under her own loose black hair, behind hands with red nails pressed over the mouth. The paint is thin and pearly, the ground bleached almost white, and the skin flushes hot around the nose and lids. Collected by the Hoki Museum.
why: Same smooth pale surface and soft even light as 森本草介 and 岡靖知, but the sitter is caught mid-feeling rather than composed — the hush pushed toward the emotional edge the collector likes in 三重野慶.

works.t: Untitled (head tilted, hair across the face)

b: Half-length figures against a bare grey-lilac wall: a child holding a small glass prism in an open palm, a young woman with a ukulele in a palm-print top. Flat frontal light, no props beyond the one object, edges softened almost to nothing. Shown at the Hoki Museum Award and collected by the Hoki Museum.
why: The stripped-down version of the 岡靖知 formula — one still figure, one soft light, nothing else — and the prism in the hand is the collector's 'figure and refracted light' motif in its most literal form.

b: Glazed oil portraits of young women — in a plum chiffon dress against a mottled plaster wall with a black-and-white cat at her knee, in profile in a peach kimono against warm brown dark, in an orange blouse before a pale damask. Layer-on-layer glazing gives the skin a lit-from-within evenness. ARC Salon finalist 2013/2014; Hoki Museum Award selection.
why: Handling worth studying next to 島村信之: the same patient glaze build-up and porcelain skin, but Hikida keeps a decorated, atmospheric ground behind the sitter instead of an empty one.

b: Paints only from the live model in the studio, never photographs, and the pictures keep the record of that: a woman holding a conch to her ear against deep blue, a woman in red at a small table with sweet peas, a woman seen from behind with her face returned by a dark mirror. The paint film is worked and slightly granular rather than licked smooth. MEXT Minister's Prize at Hakujitsu-kai; member of Hakujitsu-kai and Nitten.
why: The mirror pictures and the studio-built matière give you the 森本草介 stillness with visible paint underneath — a bridge between the hush cluster and the brushwork the collector keeps for Fechin and Schmid.

works.t: 春の香りと (With the Scent of Spring)

b: The 'Frozen Time' series: a woman seen from behind turning her head, dissolved into a near-white haze of blue and lilac so that only the shoulder blade and the line of the jaw stay sharp; elsewhere the same women sit against flat washed grounds holding flowers. Twice a Nitten Tokusen winner in his twenties, Hakujitsu-kai and Nitten member.
why: The blurred-out backgrounds and one hard-focus passage are the same optical trick Casey Baugh uses, run at 森本草介's temperature — worth having for the handling even though the sitters are often celebrities.

works.t: 東京の金魚鉢 (Tokyo Goldfish Bowl)
Frozen Time 出さなかった手紙 (The Letter I Never Sent)
あの話の続き (The Rest of That Story)
あなたがそれに気付く頃 (By the Time You Notice)

b: Young women standing or sitting in nearly bare Beijing interiors — a screen, a potted plant, a cat on the floorboards — painted with an enamel-smooth surface and a flat, almost shadowless daylight. In the later canvases the girl is set behind a pane of glass or a wall of water, with goldfish and reflections drifting across her face.
why: The closest thing China has to 森本草介: the same windless quiet, the same porcelain finish and refusal of incident — and the glass-and-water pictures do exactly what 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks do, putting a transparent barrier between you and the figure.

b: The "Paper Bride" series: a woman kneeling or standing in a wedding dress folded out of crumpled paper, lit frontally and isolated against a smoky grey-green field that dissolves at the edges. The skin is polished flat; every crease of the paper is tracked fold by fold.
why: Built exactly the way Guillermo Lorca builds a picture — one figure held in a hard light against an atmospheric nothing — but finished with 森本草介's smooth, airless surface, so it sits between the collector's two poles rather than in either.

works.t: Paper Lady (from the Paper Bride series)
Paper Bride on the shore at dusk
Paper Bride in white, hand at the chin
Paper Bride in profile, white headdress
Paper Bride in blue against night water

b: Head-and-shoulders portraits in a single grey-green key, most of them of one European sitter, Thomas, repainted for over a decade. The features are pushed almost to the edge of legibility: a pale skull-shape rising out of a ground only a shade different from the flesh, with a few darker strokes for an eye socket or a mouth.
why: The purest version of the collector's "figure seen through something" — where 三重野慶 uses steam and Alyssa Monks uses water, Mao Yan thins the paint itself into fog, and the sitter arrives already half dissolved.

b: A single figure set into a pale, dry, thinly scumbled field — a girl turning back inside a blue-grey thicket that is painted at the same pitch as her skin, or a nude on a bed under a bare hanging bulb, with drips and abraded passages left standing. The paint is scrubbed and fresco-like rather than glazed.
why: For the 三重野慶 wing of the collection: the atmosphere is not behind the figure, it is the same substance as the figure, so she has to be found in the canvas rather than read off it.

b: Women musicians in heavy silk, half-turned away, holding a cello or a pipa, set against grounds that go to near-black within a few inches of the sitter. The paint is thin and blended almost to invisibility; the whole effect is carried by the tonal drop from a warm lit cheek to the dark around it.
why: The Marlborough-era studio pictures work the way Nelson Shanks and Casey Baugh work — one warm source, deep dark surround, romance carried entirely by the light — and this is the painter who taught that formula to two generations of Chinese realists.

b: A single woman in saturated red — a bridal jacket, a shawl — dropped onto a black ground with a hard raking light from one side. The flesh is built up in thin transparent glazes over a cool underpainting; the red is left as one flat unbroken note so the whole picture turns on the collision between the two.
why: Same staging as Ken Currie and Roberto Ferri — one body cut out of a black void by a single light — played in a decorative rather than a mordant key; worth having for the glazing method, which is the most conservative Bouguereau-lineage technique still in daily use in China.

b: Two-metre-high heads of his own daughter, painted from photographs against a plain grey-green ground, with dried cotton bolls tangled into the hair. The lighting is soft and frontal, the surface is polished to no visible stroke, and the expression is held just short of anything — a child looking at you without performing.
why: The Korean answer to 岡靖知 and 島村信之: hyperreal finish used for stillness rather than for display, and the enlargement to two metres does what the collector likes in 森本草介 — it makes an ordinary quiet face into something you cannot look away from.

b: Standing figures in hanbok, painted on dark grounds that have been scraped and rubbed back to the priming at the edges, so the panel looks like a recovered object. The garment is described in full — silk, ties, the weight of a skirt — while the head is left as a smear of grey mist or hidden under a mourner's hat.
why: Does with a face what 三重野慶 does with glass and steam: the figure is present and the identity is withheld — and the dark, worn ground and single pale figure is the Ken Currie stage set used for grief rather than horror.

b: Figures whose faces are turned away, cropped off or swallowed by shadow, bodies locked into twisting poses taken from pantomime and contemporary dance. Thin, scraped paint in muted greys, ochres and dulled greens over a visible ground, with the hands, shoulders and spine carrying all the expression.
why: The performed emotion the collector kept in Kamoi Rei and Steven Assael, but routed through the body instead of the face: a figure lit against an empty dark ground with the whole drama in the pose.

b: Small oils of one figure in nocturnal or low-raking light — a sleepwalker with closed eyes pressed against a moonlit wall, a woman reading at a window, a face half-out of the dark. Thin paint, soft edges, a narrow tonal range of blue-greys and ambers, so the air in the room reads as clearly as the person.
why: This is the Morimoto/Marshennikov hush moved to a cold night: a still figure and soft light, but delivered with the cinematic atmosphere the collector wants and the calm academic realists (野田弘志, Quintanilla) lack.

b: Repin Academy graduate who emigrated to Paris in 1988 and painted the circus, the cabaret and the bullring at wall-size: white clowns, ecuyeres, Petrushka and matadors set frontally in acid yellow, ox-blood and black, laid on with heavy loaded brushwork. The stage is always literal — a lit ring, a procession, a curtain — and the performers stare straight out without smiling.
why: The closest thing the Russian school has to Kamoi Rei: despair staged as performance, a costumed figure lit against darkness, rather than the clinical anatomy (Freud, Golucho) or historical monument (Korzhev) the collector threw out.

b: Heads and half-figures at over life size, built from loose slabs and drags of oil that stay visibly wet-looking, with the face pulled into focus out of a bare, scrubbed ground. The Silent Testimony series is twenty-odd such heads of people bereaved in the Troubles, each one staring out of an unlit brown field.
why: The nearest living relative of Ken Currie: same Northern-British scale, same head lit out of darkness, same grief handled as paint rather than as anatomy.

b: Very large single figures — a woman caught in a snare of wire, a man on a broken chair, a self-portrait at nearly two metres — painted tight and cool against black, with the edges of the body dissolving where the light stops. Won the BP Portrait Award in 2008.
why: Same bargain as Steven Assael: a figure staged in the dark, described with almost photographic control but kept theatrical rather than clinical.

b: Crowds and single heavy bodies shoved together in a shallow, smoky space, painted in ochres and bitumen browns with brushwork left coarse and dragged. The recent apocalyptic pictures put a lit figure at the front of a dark, boiling mass of others.
why: The other half of the Glasgow pair with Ken Currie — anguish performed at full volume, lit against a dark ground, never dissected.

works.t: In the Forest of the Night

b: Single figures and half-length portraits on dark, thinly scraped grounds; the paint is pushed on with a knife and rag so the head resolves only from a distance. He painted a series of very old Jewish men who had lived through the war, each one alone in an unlit room.
why: The handling a painter could steal from — Fechin's loaded, scraped touch applied to a modern sitter in a dark room rather than to a Russian peasant.

b: Lamp-lit interiors where a few figures are caught mid-gesture around a table, a carcass, a puppet — flesh and cloth built in thick, wet strokes, everything else swallowed by brown dark. Several are outright banquets of meat.
why: Nick Alm's exact register — a crowded, badly-lit room painted with a loaded brush, the emotion staged rather than reported — with Assael's appetite for a theatrical group.

b: Single women, most often half-length, on flat dark grounds, with the skin carried in thin smooth layers and a cool light falling from one side. She trained with Odd Nerdrum but dropped his togas and landscapes for portrait-scale heads and shoulders.
why: A Nerdrum student who lands where Marshennikov is rather than where her teacher is: one still woman, soft even light, sealed surface, no myth machinery.

b: Large multi-figure canvases of young people in bare studio interiors, half of each body sunk in shadow, with the paint left visibly brushed and the drawing scraped back through it. Founded the Barcelona Academy of Art; his work is in the MEAM collection.
why: The Spanish equivalent of Nick Alm's crowded, lamp-lit groups — same generational subject, same bravura wet-into-wet handling with a hard dark behind it.

b: Figures placed in ordinary rooms and night-time outskirts, painted large and slightly cinematic — a boy on a wall, a self-portrait staring straight out, a body half-lost in a wood. Colour is kept low and the light comes from one weak source.
why: Delivers the Kamoi bargain in Spanish: an ordinary person staged in bad light so the mood is performed, not diagnosed — the opposite of Golucho's forensic surfaces.

works.t: Conozco un lugar en el bosque

b: Head-and-shoulders self-portraits at two or three times life size with the face smeared in wet paint — the sitter is literally coated in the medium — rendered so smoothly that every ridge of pigment reads as photograph.
why: A HUSH-cluster oddity: the sealed, poreless surface the collector likes in Morimoto and Oka, but turned on the painter's own paint-covered face.

b: Bodies falling, twisting and colliding in deep perspective boxes, modelled hard and lit from below or behind, with the compositions built from 3D models before being painted in glazed oil. The Actaeon canvases are dogs and a man tumbling through a black space.
why: Roberto Ferri's structural cousin: a nude thrown into baroque contortion and lit against darkness, but choreographed like a crash rather than a swoon.

b: Airless, high-gloss oil paintings in which a single figure — an Ottoman officer, a wounded soldier, a woman in a tiled room — sits in a light with no visible source and a surface with no visible brush. The Lost Paintings series invents nineteenth-century pictures that never existed. (His site carries an adult-content gate; the historical series is not explicit.)
why: The HUSH cluster's Turkish case: the same sealed, smooth, breath-held surface as Morimoto and Oka, with the figure held behind a film of period atmosphere.

b: Sitters at tables and in armchairs painted in thin smooth oil, with a pale gold haze pooling around the head and the edges of hands and cloth softened almost out of focus. 'An Angel At My Table', her portrait of her mother with a tea service, won the BP Portrait Award in 2018.
why: The English HUSH: a still figure in soft even light on a smooth surface, close to Morimoto — flagged as such, since the drama here is entirely in the atmosphere and not in the brush.

b: A woman alone in a dim room, built from squeegeed slabs and scraped-back oil: the paint is dragged sideways across the panel, wiped through, then a few loaded strokes put the face back. Light comes from one window or one lamp and everything else sinks into brown-black.
why: The closest living heir to Casey Baugh's atmosphere plus Richard Schmid's economy — a figure dissolving into a scraped, smoky ground, which is exactly the 'seen through something' device the collector keeps returning to.

b: Half-lit heads and single figures emerging from deep warm shadow, painted wet and fast: thick pale strokes on the lit cheek, transparent brown nothing elsewhere. Titles like 'A Heavy Weight' and 'Troubled' are literal — the sitters are shown mid-grief, shoulders collapsed.
why: The staged-despair line the collector drew when they kept Ken Currie and cut Lucian Freud: Venezia lights a suffering figure theatrically against blackness rather than dissecting it anatomically.

b: Figures built in near-monochrome greys and bone whites, the paint combed, scratched and dragged with the brush handle so the head reads as a woven or shredded surface. Faces are turned away, cropped, or veiled by the marks that describe them.
why: He literalises the collector's recurring 'figure seen THROUGH something' motif (三重野慶, Alyssa Monks) by putting the veil in the paint itself rather than in water or glass.

b: Two people at a café table, or one woman half-turned in a dark green interior, painted in low-key olive, black and cream with a loaded brush that leaves the background as open scaffolding. Nobody is looking at anybody; the titles say 'Intimate Absence', 'Crowded Silence'.
why: Richard Schmid's alla prima economy pushed toward mood rather than display — the visible handling the collector wants to learn from, but carrying real emotional weather instead of technical showmanship.

b: Close-cropped figures — a woman with her hands pressed to her chest, a head dropped into the hands — laid in with fat, ribbon-like strokes of unmixed pink, ochre and black. Backgrounds are one flat dark tone; the paint stands up off the surface in the flesh.
why: The purest example of the collector's brush pole: like Nick Alm, he lets the mark stay a mark, but the subject is always a private emotional gesture rather than a scene.

b: A single figure — usually a woman, head lowered — held together by a small area of finished face while the rest of the canvas is knifed, scraped and repainted into slabs of pink, black and bone. The drawing underneath is exact; the surface is deliberately wrecked.
why: The same negotiation Zoey Frank is on the page for — how far a figure can be broken down before it stops being a person — but Hicks keeps the head intact and grieving, so the emotional temperature survives.

b: Her long 'Homme' series is a head painted again and again in thick swirled oil until the features smear, tear open or slide off the skull; some are cool and blue, others hot orange with the mouth pulled sideways. A face is present, then wrecked, in the same picture.
why: Guillermo Lorca's theatrical violence done at portrait scale and without the fable — the performed anguish the collector kept in Kamoi, delivered by the brush rather than by narrative.

b: Alla prima portraits of tattooed, pierced friends and models, set against a plain wall or a black void and lit from one side; the dark clothing is laid in as a single mass and the whole head is resolved in a sitting. Titles like 'Black Lamb' and 'Night of the Living Dead' tell you the register.
why: The Los Angeles studio equivalent of Serge Marshennikov's stillness, but with Fechin's speed of attack — a real person, quiet, lit against dark, painted in one go.

b: Nudes wrestling, falling, or curled on the ground, painted on a warm brown ground in transparent washes with the lights struck in thickly at the end. The brown of the panel is left doing most of the shadow work; nothing is filled in.
why: He is the American atelier world's Fechin — the same open, unfinished-looking handling the collector kept Fechin and Blokhin for, applied to bodies in physical crisis rather than to costume studies.

b: Single models painted from life in one session with a big brush and almost no drawing: a head held in both hands becomes four or five wide swipes of cream, red and brown on raw ground. The figure stays legible by a hair's breadth.
why: The far end of the same road as Nick Alm — paint left as paint — and the reason to look at him next to Alm is the difference between building a figure out of marks and finding one in them.

b: A woman with her eyes closed and chin lifted, floating in a saturated blue nocturne with no room around her; elsewhere a figure sits in a half-lit apartment, the light doing all the storytelling. Surfaces are smooth and the colour is pushed to a single dominant temperature.
why: This is 森本草介's sealed quiet transposed into cinematic colour — the atmosphere that separates the hush the collector keeps from the calm academic realism they cut.

b: Large oils of women submerged in pools and lakes, painted from below or at the waterline: hair fanning against the underside of the surface, refracted bands of light crawling over a back, a face pressed close under the meniscus with air beads sitting on the skin. Everything is smooth, cool green-blue, and airless.
why: This is 三重野慶's 'seen through water' idea taken to its full extent — the same sealed, breathless stillness Morimoto gets in a room, relocated underwater; she is the closest living painter to what Alyssa Monks does with submersion, but quieter and without the shower-glass distortion.

works.t: Untitled (AQUA series), face at the waterline
Untitled (AQUA series), figure walking on the pool floor

b: Swimmers seen from underneath in green-gold lake water, the figure half dissolved by the ripple pattern above it and by the paint itself, which stays visibly brushy rather than photographic. Vintage swimsuits, bare legs, columns of bubbles.
why: The underwater half of 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks, but handled with an open, loose brush the collector already likes in Casey Baugh — the water does the softening instead of a blending brush.

b: Divers and floaters in pool water, usually shot from below so the body is read through a wall of bubbles and refracted sunlight. He paints the bubble trail as a solid mass of small light-shapes, and the skin under it stays soft-edged and warm against saturated blue.
why: The purest version of the underwater motif 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks touch on, and — like Monks — he treats the intervening medium (bubbles, not steam) as the actual subject rather than an effect on top of a portrait.

b: Close-cropped oils of a face going under, or held under: water skinned over an eye, hair plastered flat, a mouth just breaking the surface. Small panels, tight focus, and a distinctly unpleasant undertow — these are drownings as much as baths.
why: She sits exactly on the seam between the collector's two clusters: the wet-glass/wet-skin surface of 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks, carrying the performed dread they kept 鴨居玲 for — despair staged in a bathtub rather than diagnosed on an operating table.

b: Underwater figures built with a palette knife: the body is comparatively smooth, but the water around it is laid in as thick ribbons of turquoise and violet that read as light shafts. Bright, high-key, and physically thick where French and Zener are thin.
why: The same submerged-figure subject as 三重野慶 and Alyssa Monks, but delivered with loaded, visible paint — the one artist here that connects the water motif to the bravura-handling side (Nick Alm, Casey Baugh) rather than the smooth side.

b: Figures in bathtubs, beds and dark interiors painted in wet, sliding layers, so that an arm or a head appears two or three times at once and the edges of the body keep being erased by the room. The paint is thin, scraped back, and the light comes through it like light through liquid.
why: He gets the 'figure seen through something' effect from the paint itself rather than from water or glass — the closest thing on this list to what Fechin and Nick Alm do with edges, pushed until the figure is genuinely half-dissolved.

b: A single figure glimpsed inside a building from the street: a woman holding back a curtain, a man behind sash glass, seen across brick and green tile. The glass, the net curtain and the reflected sky are painted as carefully as the person, who is often the smallest and least distinct thing in the picture.
why: The most literal statement of the collector's recurring motif — the figure is always behind glass or gauze — and the muted, matte, evenly-lit surface belongs to the 森本草介 / 島村信之 side rather than the bravura side.

b: One figure, frontal, isolated on a flat grey or ochre field, with the face wiped, scraped and re-laid until the features blur into the surrounding air. Titles like 'On Darkened Stages' and 'Gone Are False Dreams' say what the pictures do: a body held in a lit void with its expression half removed.
why: Staged despair in the 鴨居玲 / Ken Currie sense — a spotlit body in an empty ground, the emotion performed rather than dissected — and the blur that takes the face is the same 'seen through something' device the collector keeps returning to.

b: Single figures on white cloth against near-empty grounds: a woman asleep face-down on rumpled linen, a body half-buried in sand, a nude seen from directly overhead. The paint surface is polished to nothing, and almost all the colour is white, sand and skin.
why: This is the Marshennikov register done in Mexico — a sleeping woman, soft even light, smooth invisible handling — but pushed further toward emptiness, so the whole picture is one body and one sheet.

b: Large canvases of one or two figures held in a warm brown half-dark — a woman lying back with her eyes shut, a dancer waiting in the wings, a widow in black. Faces and hands are worked to a high finish; the surrounding air is left broad and scumbled.
why: The closest thing Latin America has to Morimoto's sealed quiet, except the light is warm and theatrical rather than cool — the same still woman, but staged the way Steven Assael stages his sitters.

b: A nude asleep on a brown leather sofa under a white duvet, painted life-size across a wide horizontal canvas; portraits built in a single earth-green underpainting so the whole head reads as one colour with the light carved out of it.
why: The sleeping-nude canvas is Marshennikov's exact subject and light, and the verdaccio heads are the kind of visible method — one colour, then light — that made them keep Richard Schmid and Blokhin over the museum names.

works.t: Samsara Series — The Cycle of Life and Death

r: India · b. 1992 (trained Barcelona Academy of Art)
b: A swimmer floating face-up in green pool water seen from above, the body broken into ripple-shaped strokes; a dark-skinned nude lying full-length on white cloth against a flat blue wall; a head in a red dress against a red ground.
why: She paints both halves of the collection at once — the figure seen through water is Alyssa Monks' subject, and the reclining nude on white cloth is Marshennikov's, but the handling stays loose and visible rather than photographic.

r: India · b. 1991 (trained Barcelona Academy of Art)
b: Figures placed inside a specific moment and light: a girl standing in the well of a motorboat with green lagoon water above the windscreen; a bearded man in a red robe turned away from a crowded blue-walled bar; two people in white in a rowboat among water lilies at dusk.
why: The bar picture is Nick Alm's exact territory — a party painted from inside it, one figure looking out — and the boat pictures put a still figure behind glass and water the way Mieno Kei does.

r: Israel (Tel Aviv) · b. 1999 (Florence Academy of Art)
b: A woman in a thin white dress lying back along a red settee in a dim studio, bare feet over the arm, roses dropped on the floorboards; and a close view of the back of a head and shoulders, red velvet behind, the neck lit and everything else sinking into brown.
why: 'Light and Dust' is the staged interior Steven Assael would build, and 'Velvet and Gold' is a Fechin problem — a lit neck against red — solved with the paint left showing.

b: Seven women in pale nineteenth-century dresses standing hand in hand in a fog-filled winter wood; a girl in a wet white blouse against cloud, the cloth blown up behind her like a wing; a frontal head behind a bunch of dried, half-rotted flowers.
why: This is the atmosphere half of the collection — figures dissolving into weather the way Mieno Kei's do — but with a chill under it that lands nearer Ken Currie than to comfort.

b: A single figure lit cool against a flat colour field — a bare-shouldered woman holding a basket of figs and lemons in front of a grey-green wall with leaf shadows on it, or a woman in a wine-red dress sitting on wet rock among lilies in the dark.
why: The lily painting is Jeremy Lipking's setup — one woman, night vegetation, no story — and the green-wall picture keeps that cold even light the collection wants when it isn't after drama.

b: A woman in a black lace dress lying collapsed on a tiled floor, head thrown back and one arm flung out, half of her hidden behind an open wardrobe door; three girls in the same red-and-black brocade dress stacked in front of a copper-coloured eclipsed moon.
why: 'Solve' is the Kamoi Rei condition exactly — a body performing collapse for the viewer, lit and posed rather than observed — and the eclipse picture stages the same grief as tableau.

b: Small oils of people in ordinary rooms where the light is nearly gone: a soldier smoking in a red armchair against a scuffed ochre wall, a woman and a child crowded into the frame with the far side of both faces lost in shadow.
why: Blokhin's kind of picture — a figure in a shabby interior, paint left open, the mood carried entirely by how little light there is — rather than a portrait of anyone in particular.

b: Repin Academy training turned on his own mountain villages: a single Dagestani sitter — a girl wrapped in a red shawl, a boy with a basket, a woman holding a trumpet — stood against a brown-black field or an empty ridge, painted with a full, loaded brush that keeps the fabric alive while the face stays completely still.
why: The Fechin line still being worked by a living painter, but with the bravura pulled back until only the hush is left: one figure, one light, nothing behind them. Closest in feel to the collector's taste for a person staged in the dark and left there.

works.t: Girl in a red sweater with a trumpet
Girl in a red robe against a dusk sky
Girl carrying a cat over the mountains
Boy on a chair with a basket

b: Tehran rooftops and shuttered rooms, painted with a fine, almost invisible brush: a girl reading with her head bent, a woman in a brown chador holding a cup, a teenager sitting on a parapet with the city smeared out behind her. The colour is all warm brown, dust and cream, and the light is late-afternoon and low.
why: The purest living example of the 'quiet moment, one figure, weighted light' the collector keeps choosing — Morimoto's hush transposed to Iran, with the same refusal to let the sitter perform for the viewer.

works.t: Girl on a parapet above the city
Girl in a white shirt, hands at a thread
Woman on a doorstep in the sun
Women reading together in a courtyard

b: The teacher Maleki came out of, and darker than his student: old men sitting under a bare tree, boys asleep against a column, a woman sweeping a carpet through a doorway full of white glare. Thin, warm, low-key oil with a great deal of unlit space around the figure.
why: Gives the Iranian line a second, older register — the same still figure and low warm light, but with the melancholy stated outright rather than implied. Useful as the ancestor sitting behind Maleki.

works.t: Woman with her hands at her throat
Girl in a dark room, open door
Woman sweeping in the doorway light
Old man in a hat, almost swallowed by the ground

b: Oil and egg tempera on panel, worked to an enamel finish: a head thrown back with water streaming over it, a bare back with a spine of coral, a figure with a night sky growing out of its skull. Blue-black grounds, ivory flesh, everything glazed until it glows from underneath.
why: The Roberto Ferri register the collector responds to — a body staged and lit against darkness — but visionary rather than baroque, and much quieter: the despair is held in the pose and the light, not in a gesture.

works.t: Figure with branches from the head
Standing figure dissolving at the edges
Back turned, wings at the shoulders
Face lifted, water over the eyes
Standing nude with a crown of growth

b: Very large, very smooth oils of a single sitter against a flat coloured haze — sage, dusty pink, cold blue — with a patch of porcelain-blue ornament or spilled enamel painted onto the skin. No shadow anywhere, just an even, breath-held light and a face that has stopped mid-thought.
why: Contemporary Italian figuration on the cool side of Ferri: the airless, sealed stillness of Morimoto, done at wall scale. The one decorative device on the skin functions exactly like Kamoi's staging — a small artificial note inside an otherwise real quiet.

works.t: Back turned, ornament on the shoulders
Girl in a pale room, pink haze

b: Central Academy training carried to New York: half-length figures in black coats against near-black grounds, the head lit from one side and the hands doing all the work. Ochre-grey flesh, dry scumbled backgrounds, a lot of the canvas left as bare, tired colour.
why: The nearest reachable equivalent of Mao Yan's grey-fog portraiture — a Chinese painter working the same territory of a face half-lost in atmosphere — but with the melancholy of Assael's staged sitters and, unlike Mao Yan, with images that can actually be shown.

works.t: Girl in white on a bed
Woman in black with an open hand
Woman on a chair in a grey room
Woman in a black cape, hands clasped

b: Heads painted wet-into-wet and then dragged sideways while still soft, so the whole face smears into the ground — a girl haloed in yellow, a blue head half wiped away, a swimmer's head in green fog. Alla prima paint that keeps only enough drawing to be a person.
why: Exactly the 'seen through something' device the collector returns to, but the blur is in the paint rather than in glass or water. The closest available stand-in for Mao Yan's dissolving grey portraits.

works.t: Woman against a pale blue field

b: One woman in a hotel room or a bare-boarded bedroom, seen from behind or in lost profile, with all the light coming from a single sash window and the rest of the room going soft and grey. Oil and pastel, edges deliberately dissolved wherever the figure meets the air.
why: Of everything found in this pass this is the closest to the collector's core: the Morimoto hush, unaltered — a single figure in an ordinary room at an ordinary hour, backlit, saying nothing.

works.t: Woman at the window, bed in shadow
Woman standing in an empty room

b: Aymara and Afro-Bolivian sitters at more than life size, built in soft pastel worked like oil: a market woman in a knitted cap, a girl in braids in profile, an old man whose face fills the whole sheet. Plain, almost blank grounds; the entire event is the head.
why: South America beyond Lorca, and the opposite of his theatre — a single person held still and looked at for a long time. The frontal, unsmiling gravity is the Colin Davidson bargain transposed to La Paz.

works.t: Woman in white beneath a tree

b: Slow, tightly finished oils of one young woman — head wrapped in yellow or red cloth, a robin sitting on the fabric, pigeons standing on her hair, a bare figure crouched on a stone block against a blue-grey sea. Old-master surface, contemporary blankness of expression.
why: Latin America filled with something other than Lorca's spectacle: the theatre here is one prop and one animal, and everything else is held still. The staged-but-silent register the collector kept in Kamoi.
